title: /æ/ vs /e/ vs /ɜː/
explain: Mandarin has no /æ/ and no /ɜː/. All three collapse toward one mid vowel, so bad / bed / bird sound nearly identical.
note: Mandarin vowel space has no open front /æ/ nor central r-coloured /ɜː/.

title: /iː/ vs /ɪ/
explain: Mandarin /i/ is one category. English splits it into tense /iː/ (long, tight) and lax /ɪ/ (short, relaxed).
note: It's not just length — tongue position and tension differ too.

title: /uː/ vs /ʊ/
explain: Same tense/lax problem on the back vowels. /ʊ/ (the short, relaxed one) is usually the missing one.
note: Parallel to the /iː/–/ɪ/ split.

title: /ʌ/ vs /ɑː/ vs /ɒ/
explain: Three distinct English vowels map onto roughly one region in Mandarin — frequently merged.
note: Mandarin 'a' covers ground English splits three ways.

title: schwa /ə/
explain: The most frequent vowel in English barely exists in Mandarin. Learners give every syllable a full, clear vowel instead of reducing unstressed ones to /ə/.
note: Root cause of weak-form difficulty — see the Stress & Rhythm cards.

title: /θ/ and /ð/
explain: Neither exists in Mandarin. Usually replaced: think→'sink' (/s/), this→'dis' (/d/ or /z/). The tongue-between-teeth gesture feels unnatural.
note: No dental fricatives in Mandarin's inventory.

title: /v/ vs /w/
explain: Standard Mandarin has no /v/. Replaced with /w/ (very→'wery') or /f/. This is exactly why 'I've' was hard — the final /v/ has no native template.
note: Connects directly to the I've / I'll / I'm work.

title: /n/ vs /l/
explain: Many southern Mandarin dialects merge /n/ and /l/, so speakers from those regions may swap them in English too.
note: Dialect-dependent; strong in 湖南, 四川, parts of 福建 etc.

title: English /r/
explain: Mandarin's 'r' (日 sound) is a different gesture. English /r/ has no tongue contact and often colours the vowel (car, bird). Learners substitute the Mandarin retroflex.
note: Different articulation + r-colouring of vowels is unfamiliar.

title: Final stops /p t k b d g/
explain: The single biggest structural problem. Mandarin syllables end only in a vowel, /n/, or /ŋ/. English final consonants get a vowel added (epenthesis): bed→'bedduh', map→'mappuh'.
note: Why months, asked, I've all felt hard — Mandarin can't end a syllable that way.

title: Voiced vs voiceless finals
explain: Mandarin has no voiced/voiceless contrast at the end of a syllable. The key cue in English is actually vowel length (the vowel before /d/ is longer than before /t/) — a cue learners don't use.
note: Listeners miss the contrast because they're listening for the wrong cue.

title: Consonant clusters
explain: Mandarin has zero consonant clusters. English piles them up (str-, -ksts). Learners insert vowels to break them up: street→'si-tu-reet'.
note: No native cluster template; epenthesis is the fallback.

title: Dark /l/ (word-final)
explain: The 'dark' /l/ at the end of a word needs the tongue tip to land on the ridge. Often replaced by a vowel glide or dropped. This is the I'll problem.
note: Tongue-tip contact, not just a glide.

title: Word stress
explain: English moves stress to change meaning or part of speech, and unstressed syllables reduce. Mandarin gives each syllable full weight, so learners stress evenly.
note: Wrong stress is often less intelligible than a wrong vowel.

title: Stress-timing (rhythm)
explain: English squeezes unstressed syllables to keep a steady beat on the stressed ones. Mandarin gives every syllable roughly equal time. This is the root of weak forms and connected speech.
note: Why a-cup-of-tea compresses to 'uh-CUP-uh-tea' — and why it's hard.

title: Sentence intonation
explain: Mandarin tones operate on single syllables; English intonation rises and falls across a whole phrase. The two systems interfere — learners may sound flat or place pitch movement oddly.
note: Phrase-level melody vs syllable-level tone.

title: Tone interference
explain: Some learners unconsciously assign Mandarin tones to English syllables, producing a sing-song pattern that native English listeners hear as unusual emphasis.
note: Carrying the native tone system onto the target language.

title: -ed endings  /t/ /d/ /ɪd/
explain: Past -ed is one of three sounds, chosen by the sound before it: voiceless → /t/ (walked), voiced → /d/ (played), t or d → /ɪd/ (wanted). Mandarin speakers often drop it — both because Chinese marks the past with context/particles, not endings, AND because it adds a hard final consonant or cluster.
note: Bridges grammar (tense) and root cause 2 (syllable endings). Hearing walk vs walked retrains the ear.

title: -s / -es endings  /s/ /z/ /ɪz/
explain: Plural and 3rd-person -s is also three sounds: voiceless → /s/ (cats), voiced → /z/ (dogs), sibilant → /ɪz/ (buses). Dropped for the same two reasons as -ed: Mandarin marks neither number nor agreement, and the final consonant is hard to land.
note: Same rule shape as -ed — drill them together.

title: Voicing vs aspiration (p/b · t/d · k/g)
explain: Mandarin contrasts aspirated vs unaspirated; English contrasts voiced vs voiceless. The two systems don't line up, so word-initial p/b, t/d, k/g get confused.
note: A perception problem like bed/bad — train the ear before the mouth.
